title: Birthright Citizenship & the 14th Amendment
hook: Born on U.S. soil, you're a citizen — full stop, according to the Constitution's plain text. In 2026 the Supreme Court reaffirmed that even a presidential order can't rewrite it.
key_points: The 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause grants citizenship to (almost) everyone born on U.S. soil — a rule called jus soli.
This 'right of the soil' contrasts with jus sanguinis, citizenship inherited through a parent, used by many other countries.
In 2025 the administration issued an order narrowing birthright citizenship for children of some noncitizens.
In June 2026 the Supreme Court struck down that order, per SCOTUSblog.
The ruling reaffirms that changing a constitutional rule takes more than an executive order.
content_html: Few constitutional rules sound as simple as this one: if you are born on U.S. soil, you are a U.S. citizen. That rule, known as jus soli ("right of the soil"), comes from the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause, ratified in 1868 to guarantee citizenship to formerly enslaved people and their children regardless of what any state law said.
extra_html: Jus soli is not universal — many countries instead use jus sanguinis ("right of blood"), passing citizenship down through a parent regardless of birthplace, or some blend of both. In 2025, the U.S. administration issued an executive order attempting to narrow birthright citizenship, denying it to children born in the U.S. to parents who are undocumented or on certain temporary visas. According to SCOTUSblog's Amy Howe, the Supreme Court struck down that order in June 2026. Whatever one thinks of the underlying policy question, the case is a clean illustration of a basic constitutional principle: a rule written into the Constitution's text cannot simply be redefined by executive order — changing it would ordinarily require a constitutional amendment or a fresh ruling reinterpreting the text itself, not a unilateral instruction from the executive branch. (This card describes the U.S. constitutional rule specifically; other countries assign citizenship at birth under very different rules.)

related.title: What Citizenship Is
related.hook: Citizenship is the formal bond between a person and a state — the status that turns a resident into a full member, with rights and duties to match.

related.title: Immigration & Naturalization
related.hook: Every state has to answer two charged questions: who gets to come in, and who gets to become one of us? That's the politics of immigration and citizenship.

related.title: Due Process
related.hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'jus soli' mean, and where does it come from in U.S. law?
flashcards.back_html: "Right of the soil" — citizenship granted to (almost) anyone born on U.S. territory. It comes from the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause, ratified in 1868.

flashcards.prompt: How does jus soli differ from jus sanguinis?

choices.text: Jus soli grants citizenship by birthplace; jus sanguinis grants it through a parent
They are two names for the same rule
Jus sanguinis only applies to naturalized citizens

flashcards.explanation_html: Jus soli looks at where you were born; jus sanguinis looks at your parents' citizenship, regardless of birthplace.

flashcards.prompt: What did the Supreme Court do in June 2026 regarding birthright citizenship?

choices.text: It struck down an executive order that tried to narrow it
It required Congress to redefine citizenship by statute

flashcards.explanation_html: Per SCOTUSblog, the Court struck down the administration's order — reaffirming that a constitutional rule can't be rewritten by executive order alone.
